chunks: Welcome to your lesson on recursion. Let us break it down clearly.
At its core, recursion means a function calls itself to solve a smaller version of the exact same problem.
Every recursive function must have two critical parts: a base case that stops the recursion, and a recursive step that moves closer to that base case.
Think of it like calculating factorial of 3: you calculate 3 times factorial of 2, which is 2 times factorial of 1.
Once factorial of 1 hits the base case, each waiting function gets its answer and completes, unwinding the call stack.
Let us look at how your computer keeps track of function calls using the call stack.
The call stack operates on a Last-In, First-Out principle, exactly like a stack of plates in a dining hall.
Whenever you call a function, a new stack frame is pushed on top containing local variables and return address.
When a function returns its value, its frame is immediately popped off the top.
If recursive calls keep piling up without stopping, the stack runs out of allocated space, causing a stack overflow.
Today we focus on the most important line in any recursive algorithm: the base case.
The base case is your stopping condition. It answers the problem directly without making any further recursive calls.
Without an explicit base case, your function would invoke itself forever until the execution stack crashes.
Always check your base case condition first before executing the recursive call.
